title: Custom or ready-made: when to build your own bat
seo_title: Custom vs ready-made table tennis bats: when to switch
description: When to swap a ready-made table tennis bat for a custom one: what changes, what it costs, how to glue rubbers on legally and how often to replace them.
summary: A ready-made bat is the right start, but most regular players soon build their own from a blade and two rubbers. Here is when to make the move, what it costs and how it is done.
key_points: Start with a ready-made bat; switch to custom once you play every week and your rubber has worn out.
Cheap ready-made bats are not designed to have their rubbers replaced, so a worn one means a new bat.
A custom bat lets you choose the blade and each rubber, and replace the rubbers when they wear.
Glue rubbers on with water-based, solvent-free glue, trim them to the edge of the blade and keep the ITTF logo near the handle.
Butterfly's rule of thumb: change your rubbers as many times a year as you play each week.
body: Build your own bat once you are playing every week, your strokes are settling down and your ready-made bat's rubber has lost its grip. A custom bat is a blade and two rubbers bought separately and glued together, so you can choose each part and replace the rubbers when they wear. For your first months, a ready-made bat is the better buy: cheaper, simpler and good enough to learn on.
## What the difference is

A ready-made bat, sometimes called pre-assembled, comes with the rubbers already glued on. Butterfly says its recreational ones "simplify the buying process as the rubber is already assembled", so there is no need to study blade and rubber charts. Table Tennis England, the sport's governing body in England, recommends a ready-made bat for beginners, though it notes that others advise against it. Our guide to [what bat to buy](/guide/what-table-tennis-bat-to-buy.html) covers that first choice.

A custom bat starts with a bare [blade](/guide/table-tennis-blades-explained.html), the wooden part, and two rubbers, one for each side. You pick the speed of the blade, the shape of the handle, and the type, thickness and hardness of each rubber.
## The catch with cheap ready-made bats

On most cheap bats the rubber is there for life. Butterfly says that on its recreational bats "the rubber is not meant to be removed", and that when it needs replacing, "it's time to toss the old racket and buy a new one". Its dearer Pro-Line ready-made bats use a glue that lets you peel the old rubber off and fit new sheets, which makes them a halfway house.
## When to switch

Three signs tell you it is time. First, you play every week, at a club or in a league. Second, you can play the basic strokes with control and want more speed or spin than your bat gives. Third, your rubber is wearing out: Butterfly says a worn rubber "will produce less spin than it once did and will not feel as lively". Table Tennis England says a custom bat "will definitely raise your playing ability", but there is no rush. If you play once a month, a good ready-made bat will last for years.
## Choosing the parts

Keep your first custom bat close to what you know. An allround blade made only of wood, and the same smooth rubber on both sides, in a medium sponge thickness of around 1.7mm to 1.9mm, is a sensible first set-up. Our guides to [rubbers](/guide/table-tennis-rubbers-explained.html) and [sponge thickness and hardness](/guide/rubber-sponge-thickness-hardness.html) explain the options, and the coach at your club is worth asking before you buy.
## What it costs

At UK retailers, a ready-made bat from a main brand starts at about £20 to £45 for a recreational model. Butterfly's better ready-made bats, with replaceable rubbers, cost roughly £70 to £150. For a custom bat, an allround blade costs about £25 to £55, and each rubber about £35 to £60, with top-end rubbers up to £90. Add a tube of glue at about £8 to £15. A modest first custom bat therefore costs around £100 to £120 in all.
## Gluing it yourself

Many shops will assemble a custom bat for you, often free when you buy the blade and rubbers together. Doing it yourself is not hard, and you will need to when the rubbers wear out. The steps from Butterfly and Stiga are broadly the same:

Clean any old glue off the blade. Spread a thin, even layer of water-based glue over the sponge side of the rubber and over the blade. Leave both until the glue turns from milky white to clear, about 20 minutes. Lay the rubber on starting from the handle end and press it down firmly and evenly, avoiding air bubbles. Then turn the bat over, sponge side up, and trim the excess rubber with sharp scissors, cutting flush against the edge of the blade. Stiga and Butterfly both suggest edge tape to protect the rim. Makers differ on rollers: Stiga suggests one, while Butterfly's assembly guide says to press by hand.
## What the rules say

If you play in leagues or tournaments, your home-made bat must follow the ITTF Laws. Each rubber must be on the ITTF's authorised list and fixed so that the ITTF logo, the maker's name and brand are clearly visible nearest the handle, so position the logo before you press it down. The rubber must extend "up to but not beyond the limits of the blade", which is why you trim it to the edge. And the Regulations make it your responsibility to use glue that does not contain harmful volatile solvents. Water-based glues from the main makers are designed for this. Our guide to [approved rubbers and the racket rules](/guide/ittf-approved-rubbers-and-racket-rules.html) explains the rest.
## Looking after it

Clean the rubbers after each session, keep them covered with protective film and keep the bat in a case, out of sunlight and heat. Rubbers wear far faster than blades. Butterfly's rule of thumb is that the number of days you play each week equals the number of times a year you should change your rubbers: play twice a week, and replace them about every six months.
When you are ready to look beyond your first rubbers, read [Chinese tacky against European tensor rubbers](/guide/tacky-vs-tensor-rubbers.html).
